content.content:
1	Temperature-sensitive goods such as vaccines, biological samples, prepared meals and laboratory reagents are frequently shipped in insulated carriers that hold a payload within a target temperature band for a period of hours or days. Carriers of this general kind fall into two broad families. Powered carriers use a fan, a pump or another driven air mover, together with a power source, to force air over a cold source and through the payload space. Passive carriers omit the power source and rely on conduction from, and natural convection around, a refrigerant mass such as water ice, dry ice, gel packs or sealed cassettes charged with a phase-change material.
2	
3	Passive carriers are attractive because they have no battery to charge, no motor to fail and no electrical approval burden for air transport. They are also harder to control. When a refrigerant mass is simply laid on top of, beside or beneath a payload, the cooled air falls where gravity and the packing arrangement happen to send it. Items directly against the refrigerant are driven toward the cold end of the acceptable band or below it, while items on the far side of the payload sit in a stagnant warm layer. The result is a temperature spread across the payload that grows as the load is packed more densely, and that varies from shipment to shipment because it depends on how a particular packer arranged the goods and the refrigerant on a particular day.
4	
5	Attempts to impose a defined circulation path on a passive carrier run into a practical difficulty. The path is defined by clearances, by openings and by the alignment between them, and every one of those relationships is destroyed if the component that carries the openings is set down rotated, offset or skewed by a person working quickly at a packing bench. A carrier that circulates air well when it is assembled precisely, and poorly when it is not, delivers the variability it was intended to remove. Packing instructions, printed arrows and keyed corner blocks all depend on the packer looking, and none of them acts on a component that has already been set down out of position.
6	
7	Two further problems attend repeated reuse of a passive carrier. First, moist ambient air admitted each time the carrier is opened condenses on the cold surfaces of the refrigerant mass and runs down into the payload space, wetting labels and cartons and, over many cycles, leaving standing water in the base of the carrier. Where the refrigerant is a sealed cassette, drying the interior often means removing the cassette from service. Second, a passive carrier gives no account of itself. If the payload was exposed to a temperature excursion in transit, and the refrigerant has since recovered, an inspection at the receiving dock shows a cold carrier and a firm cassette, and the excursion leaves no trace. Electronic data loggers record such events but add cost, battery management and a reading step to every unit shipped, and they report a sensor location rather than the state of the refrigerant that the payload actually depends on.
8	
9	There remains a need for a reusable passive carrier that establishes the same circulation path around the payload every time it is closed, without a powered air mover and without relying on the care of the person who packed it, that manages the condensate produced by repeated opening without taking the refrigerant out of service, and that retains a visible mechanical record of a refrigerant temperature excursion after the refrigerant has recovered.
10

file.content:
Temperature-sensitive goods such as vaccines, biological samples, prepared meals and laboratory reagents are frequently shipped in insulated carriers that hold a payload within a target temperature band for a period of hours or days. Carriers of this general kind fall into two broad families. Powered carriers use a fan, a pump or another driven air mover, together with a power source, to force air over a cold source and through the payload space. Passive carriers omit the power source and rely on conduction from, and natural convection around, a refrigerant mass such as water ice, dry ice, gel packs or sealed cassettes charged with a phase-change material.

Passive carriers are attractive because they have no battery to charge, no motor to fail and no electrical approval burden for air transport. They are also harder to control. When a refrigerant mass is simply laid on top of, beside or beneath a payload, the cooled air falls where gravity and the packing arrangement happen to send it. Items directly against the refrigerant are driven toward the cold end of the acceptable band or below it, while items on the far side of the payload sit in a stagnant warm layer. The result is a temperature spread across the payload that grows as the load is packed more densely, and that varies from shipment to shipment because it depends on how a particular packer arranged the goods and the refrigerant on a particular day.

Attempts to impose a defined circulation path on a passive carrier run into a practical difficulty. The path is defined by clearances, by openings and by the alignment between them, and every one of those relationships is destroyed if the component that carries the openings is set down rotated, offset or skewed by a person working quickly at a packing bench. A carrier that circulates air well when it is assembled precisely, and poorly when it is not, delivers the variability it was intended to remove. Packing instructions, printed arrows and keyed corner blocks all depend on the packer looking, and none of them acts on a component that has already been set down out of position.

Two further problems attend repeated reuse of a passive carrier. First, moist ambient air admitted each time the carrier is opened condenses on the cold surfaces of the refrigerant mass and runs down into the payload space, wetting labels and cartons and, over many cycles, leaving standing water in the base of the carrier. Where the refrigerant is a sealed cassette, drying the interior often means removing the cassette from service. Second, a passive carrier gives no account of itself. If the payload was exposed to a temperature excursion in transit, and the refrigerant has since recovered, an inspection at the receiving dock shows a cold carrier and a firm cassette, and the excursion leaves no trace. Electronic data loggers record such events but add cost, battery management and a reading step to every unit shipped, and they report a sensor location rather than the state of the refrigerant that the payload actually depends on.

There remains a need for a reusable passive carrier that establishes the same circulation path around the payload every time it is closed, without a powered air mover and without relying on the care of the person who packed it, that manages the condensate produced by repeated opening without taking the refrigerant out of service, and that retains a visible mechanical record of a refrigerant temperature excursion after the refrigerant has recovered.

1	A passive cold-chain carrier is disclosed in which the closing of the lid, rather than the care of the packer, establishes the circulation path.
2	
3	In one aspect, the carrier includes an insulated outer shell having a floor and side walls, a product tray removably received in the outer shell, a thermal module removably received in the outer shell above the product tray, and an insulated lid. The product tray is supported above the floor by tray feet so that a lower return passage remains between the product tray and the floor, and the tray side walls are spaced inward from the side walls of the outer shell to form two side supply passages. The thermal module includes a rigid spacer frame and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame, the spacer frame defining a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings. The insulated lid carries a depending indexing rib positioned to enter a mating channel of the spacer frame as the lid closes and to shift the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages.
4	
5	In the registered position the shell, the product tray, the thermal module and the lid cooperate to define a circulation path along which air rising from a product region within the product tray enters the central inlet opening, divides along faces of the two phase-change cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage. The carrier is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover.
6	
7	The technical effect of lid-driven registration is that the alignment on which the circulation path depends is created by an act the packer cannot omit. The thermal module is placed in the outer shell above the product tray, and the depending indexing rib entering the mating channel shifts the module into the position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages. The seal made by a compressible lid gasket against the upper edge of the outer shell occurs after registration, so the carrier is not closed against a module that is still out of position. The same closing movement presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the outer shell, so that the registered module is held down against the product tray and cannot lift away from it under the vibration and inversion of transport.
8	
9	In a further aspect, a shallow condensate channel extends around the product tray and receives a removable absorbent wick. Discharge openings at lower ends of the guide ducts deliver condensate into the condensate channel. A pull tab on the absorbent wick remains accessible when the product tray is removed, so the wick is replaced without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service.
10	
11	In a further aspect, the outer shell carries a mechanical exposure indicator visible from outside the carrier. An indicator stem is thermally coupled to one of the phase-change cassettes and is retained by a temperature-responsive latch. If that cassette softens enough to release the latch, a spring moves the indicator stem to a latched exposed position, and the indication remains exposed after the cassette cools again, being reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The indicator therefore reports the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends, survives recovery of the cassette, and requires no battery. The exposure indicator does not control airflow, so the circulation path is unaffected by whether the indicator has tripped.
12	
13	In a further aspect, a method includes fitting conditioned phase-change cassettes to the spacer frame, placing product in the product tray, placing the product tray in the outer shell, placing the thermal module above the product tray, and closing the insulated lid so that the depending indexing rib enters the mating channel and shifts the thermal module into the registered position, whereafter air circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover.
14	
15	The features summarised above may be used together or separately, and the summary is not a statement of the scope of the claims.

The exposure indicator does not control airflow, so the circulation path is unaffected by whether the indicator has tripped.

The features summarised above may be used together or separately, and the summary is not a statement of the scope of the claims.

The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.
6	
7	The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.
8	
9	The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. The tray side walls 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.
10	
11	The thermal module
12	
13	Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 before packing.
14	
15	The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, each guide duct 50 located beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 aligned with the side supply passages 28.
16	
17	The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.
18	
19	Registration and retention by the lid
20	
21	The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.
22	
23	This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and the registration is completed by the closing of the lid. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is therefore created by an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.
24	
25	The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.
26	
27	The circulation path
28	
29	In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20, from which it rises again through the product region.
30	
31	The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Air warmed in the product region rises to the central inlet opening 48, and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes descends through the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, so that circulation proceeds without any powered air mover.
32	
33	Condensate management
34	
35	A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough formed in the outer shell 10 and extending around the product tray 20. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. Discharge openings 76 are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.
36	
37	The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.
38	
39	Mechanical exposure indicator
40	
41	The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. Referring to FIG. 6, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44.
42	
43	The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.
44	
45	The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.
46	
47	The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.
48	
49	Operation
50	
51	In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Goods are placed in the product tray 20 and the product tray 20 is placed in the outer shell 10 so that the tray feet 22 stand on the floor 12, leaving the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20 and the two side supply passages 28 between the tray side walls 26 and the side walls 14. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20. The insulated lid 60 is then closed, whereby the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 and shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position, the resilient feet 58 are pressed against the ledges 18 to retain the thermal module 40, and the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. Air thereafter circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.
52	
53	Essential and optional features
54	
55	Two phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42, opposed across the central space. Entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.
56	
57	The described implementations are examples. A person skilled in the art may combine, substitute or omit the described features within the scope of the claims that follow.

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and the registration is completed by the closing of the lid. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is therefore created by an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough formed in the outer shell 10 and extending around the product tray 20. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

Mechanical exposure indicator

The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. Referring to FIG. 6, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.

Essential and optional features

Two phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42, opposed across the central space. Entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.

1. A passive cold-chain carrier comprising:

an insulated outer shell having a floor, side walls and an upper edge;

a product tray removably received in the outer shell, the product tray having a bottom wall, tray side walls, perforations, and tray feet standing on the floor so that the product tray is supported above the floor and a lower return passage remains between the bottom wall and the floor, the tray side walls being spaced inward from the side walls of the outer shell so that two side supply passages are formed;

a thermal module removably received in the outer shell above the product tray, the thermal module comprising a rigid spacer frame and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame, the spacer frame defining a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts located beside the phase-change cassettes, peripheral outlet openings aligned with the side supply passages, and a mating channel; and

an insulated lid closable on the upper edge of the outer shell and carrying a depending indexing rib positioned to enter the mating channel as the insulated lid closes and to shift the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages;

the carrier being free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover, and the outer shell, the product tray, the thermal module and the insulated lid cooperating in the registered position to define a circulation path along which air rising from a product region within the product tray enters the central inlet opening, divides along faces of the two phase-change cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through the perforations, and returns through the lower return passage.

2. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the spacer frame carries resilient feet, the outer shell has ledges beneath the resilient feet, and closure of the insulated lid presses the resilient feet against the ledges so that the thermal module is held down against lifting away from the product tray.

3. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, further comprising a compressible lid gasket carried by the insulated lid and arranged to seal against the upper edge of the outer shell after the depending indexing rib has shifted the thermal module into the registered position.

4. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the two opposed phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame with an inner face of a first phase-change cassette confronting an inner face of a second phase-change cassette across a central space, and the central inlet opening opens downward into the central space.

5. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame.

6. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, further comprising a shallow condensate channel extending around the product tray, and a removable absorbent wick lying in the condensate channel.

7. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 6, wherein the spacer frame further defines discharge openings at lower ends of the guide ducts, the discharge openings discharging condensate into the condensate channel.

8. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 6, wherein the absorbent wick carries a pull tab that remains accessible when the product tray is removed from the outer shell, so that the absorbent wick is replaceable without opening a phase-change cassette.

9. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, further comprising a mechanical exposure indicator carried by the outer shell and visible from outside the carrier, the mechanical exposure indicator comprising an indicator stem thermally coupled to one of the phase-change cassettes, a temperature-responsive latch retaining the indicator stem in a stowed position, and a spring biasing the indicator stem toward an exposed position, the temperature-responsive latch releasing the indicator stem when said one of the phase-change cassettes softens.

10. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 9, wherein the exposed position is a latched position in which the mechanical exposure indicator retains the indicator stem after said one of the phase-change cassettes has cooled again, the mechanical exposure indicator being resettable manually only after the carrier is opened.

11. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 9, wherein the mechanical exposure indicator does not control airflow, the circulation path being the same whether or not the indicator stem stands in the exposed position.

12. The passive cold-chain carrier of claim 1, wherein the depending indexing rib meets the mating channel while the insulated lid is spaced above the upper edge of the outer shell, and remaining closing travel of the insulated lid translates the spacer frame horizontally into the registered position.

a rigid spacer frame sized to be removably received in the outer shell above the product tray; and

two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame;

15. The thermal module of claim 13, wherein the mating channel opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame.

16. The thermal module of claim 13, wherein the spacer frame further defines discharge openings at lower ends of the guide ducts and positioned to discharge condensate into a condensate channel of the outer shell.

17. A method of transporting temperature-sensitive goods, the method comprising:

fitting two conditioned phase-change cassettes to a rigid spacer frame of a thermal module, the spacer frame defining a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts located beside the phase-change cassettes, peripheral outlet openings aligned with the side supply passages, and a mating channel;

placing the goods in a product tray and placing the product tray in an insulated outer shell so that tray feet of the product tray stand on a floor of the outer shell, leaving a lower return passage between the product tray and the floor and two side supply passages between tray side walls of the product tray and side walls of the outer shell;

This continuing space is one of the side supply passages 28.

A thin hatched horizontal bottom wall joins the thin upright wall and extends rightward, and the open space beneath that bottom wall is the lower return passage 24.

# FIG. 1

Schematic vertical sectional view of an assembled passive cold-chain carrier. Plain black line work on white, section hatching on cut material, all line work inside the drawing area.

Two thick hatched upright wall bodies joined at the bottom by a thick hatched horizontal bottom body form an upright container, open at the top. These are the sectioned outer shell 10, its bottom body being the floor 12. A block projects inward from each wall body below its top end.

A thick hatched horizontal slab across the top ends of both wall bodies is the insulated lid 60, closed. A narrow rib projects downward from its underside inboard of the left wall body top end, and a small compressible body lies between the slab and each top end.

Inside the container, a sectioned open-top box with thin hatched upright walls and a bottom wall is the product tray 20. Its bottom wall is raised above the floor 12 and its outer side surfaces stand clear of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap on each side. Small openings pass through each upright wall below the bottom wall level, and each upright wall stops short of the floor 12.

Two short hatched blocks between the tray bottom wall and the floor 12 are the tray feet 22. The open space between that wall and the floor 12 is the lower return passage 24. A shallow upwardly open trough in the floor 12 at each gap foot holds an elongated absorbent body.

Between the open top of the product tray 20 and the lid 60, an elongated hatched body drawn in section is the thermal module 40. Two upright plain rectangular blocks, shown schematically, stand within it, spaced from one another and from its ends. The body is open downward at its centre, and an open vertical channel runs down through it outboard of each block, opening through its outboard side above the gap. An upwardly open groove in its top surface receives the lower end of the narrow rib.

Three thin broken-line closed curves enclose the upper left region with the rib, groove and left wall top; the lower left region with the outboard channel opening, the left gap and the tray openings; and the region with the trough and absorbent body. They indicate the regions enlarged in FIGS. 3, 4 and 5.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10: outside the container, with a lead line and arrow to the outer shell as a whole.
- 12: well inside the bottom body.
- 20: well inside the left upright wall of the box.
- 22: inside the left short block.
- 24: inside the space beneath the tray bottom wall.
- 40: outside the container, with a lead line and arrow to the module as a whole.
- 60: well inside the slab at the top.
- 100: outside the container, with a lead line and arrow to the whole carrier.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged view of a lower side region of FIG. 1, seen horizontally in section. Plain black line work on white, section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

A thick hatched upright insulating wall body occupies the left portion of the drawing area and runs the full height of the fragment, its inner surface facing right. This fragment is taken at a position along that wall between the ledges of the outer shell, so no ledge appears in this view.

In the upper right part of the drawing area, a hatched body fragment is drawn in section. Its left face is spaced from the inner surface of the upright wall body, leaving an open vertical space between them. An open vertical channel passes down through this fragment, bounded by hatched material to its left and right. This channel is one of the guide ducts 50.

Where that channel meets the open vertical space, an opening passes through the left face of the body fragment, so that the channel opens sideways into that space between the fragment and the upright wall body. This opening is one of the peripheral outlet openings 54.

Below the body fragment, and spaced to the right of the inner surface of the upright wall body, a thin hatched upright wall is drawn in section and runs downward to the lower edge of the fragment. This thin wall is one of the tray side walls 26. The open vertical space continues down between the upright wall body and the thin wall, so that the space fed through the peripheral outlet opening 54 runs downward past the thin wall. This continuing space is one of the side supply passages 28.

A thin hatched horizontal bottom wall joins the thin upright wall and extends rightward, and the open space beneath that bottom wall is the lower return passage 24.

In the portion of the thin upright wall below that bottom wall, a series of small openings passes through it, so that the side supply passage 28 opens through them into the space beneath the bottom wall. These openings are the perforations 30.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 24: inside the open space beneath the thin horizontal bottom wall.
- 26: well inside the hatching of the thin upright wall, above the small openings.
- 28: inside the open vertical space between the upright wall body and the thin wall.
- 30: on one of the small openings in the thin upright wall.
- 50: inside the open vertical channel in the body fragment.
- 54: on the opening through the left face of the body fragment.

The draft is now clean against both preflight failures. Summary of what I did:

**Review items fixed**
- `draft/07-drawings.md` and `figures/FIG-1.md` used the form "FIGS. 3, 4 and 5". The preflight parsed the trailing "4" and "5" as undefined reference numerals with no figure appearance. Both now read "FIG. 3, in FIG. 4 and in FIG. 5", so every digit in the specification is either a defined numeral or an explicit figure reference.
- `figures/FIG-4.md` carried the negative linework control "so no ledge appears in this view". It now states the required geometry positively: the wall body's inner surface is a flat vertical surface running straight from the top of the fragment to the bottom.

**Two small defects I corrected while in those files**
- `figures/FIG-5.md` had a run-on clause ("...upright wall body its lower edge stopping short of...") that made the spacing relationship ambiguous to a renderer; added the missing comma.
- `figures/FIG-2.md` and `figures/FIG-6.md` described hidden structure by saying it "is not drawn" / "is omitted". Both are now positive occlusion statements naming what is visible, so neither can be read as a generic linework ban.
- Claim 17 recited "peripheral outlet openings aligned with the side supply passages" in its first step, before the side supply passages were introduced in the second step. Removed the premature phrase; the registered-position step later in the same claim already ties the openings to the passages, so scope is unchanged and antecedent basis is clean.

Everything else in the body text I left alone.

input.summary: Cleared the two mechanical preflight failures and fixed three defects found while doing so. The bare "4" and "5" that the numeral checker complained about came from the phrase "FIGS. 3, 4 and 5" in the Brief Description of the Drawings and in the FIG. 1 brief; both now spell out each figure reference, so no digit in the specification is loose. The FIG. 4 brief's negative control "so no ledge appears in this view" is replaced by a positive statement of the wall's flat inner surface. I also repaired a run-on clause in the FIG. 5 brief, converted two "is not drawn" / "is omitted" statements in the FIG. 2 and FIG. 6 briefs into positive occlusion statements, and removed a premature reference to "the side supply passages" from the first step of method claim 17 where they had no antecedent. No body text, claim scope, disclosure content or numeral assignment was otherwise touched. One thing the user should know: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references at all, so the Background carries no citations and there was no art to draft around. As the brief warned, no prior-art search was run for this application, and the art available here is not merely possibly incomplete, it is empty. The claims were written from the disclosure alone and have not been tested against any reference. A search should be run before filing.
reasoning: The numeral checker's complaint about 4 and 5 was a real defect in the text, not a false positive in substance. Its regex consumes 'FIGS. 3' and then sees ', 4 and 5' as bare integers, which in a patent specification is exactly the pattern of an undefined reference numeral. Writing each figure reference out in full is the conservative fix: it satisfies the check and is also the more formal usage.

The FIG. 4 brief said the fragment was taken between the ledges so no ledge appears. That sentence existed to stop the renderer drawing a shelf into the wall, which is a renderer control rather than invention geometry. I replaced it with the affirmative fact the drawing actually needs, that the inner surface of the wall body is flat and continuous over the height of the fragment. Nothing about the ledges 18 changed; they remain shown in FIG. 3, where they carry the resilient feet 58.

I did not restructure the claim set or the description. The request was to write the draft and the reviewer found only mechanical faults, so widening the edit would have destroyed working text for nothing.

Claim 1 rests on the feature that carries the whole application: the depending indexing rib on the lid entering the mating channel of the spacer frame during closing travel and shifting the module into a registered position where the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages. That is the disclosed essential relationship, it does real technical work because the circulation path exists only when that overlap exists, and it is the alignment step that a passive carrier otherwise leaves to the packer. The full circulation path and the absence of any powered air mover are recited with it because the disclosure states both as essential.

Deliberately left out of claim 1: the compressible lid gasket, the resilient feet and ledges, the condensate channel, the wick and its pull tab, and the mechanical exposure indicator. The disclosure marks the wick and the indicator as optional, and the gasket and the retention feet, although disclosed as part of the closing sequence, are not needed for the registered path to exist. Each of them is a dependent claim instead, so the ladder retreats first to retention (claim 2), then sealing order (claim 3), then cassette geometry (claims 4 and 5), then condensate management (claims 6 to 8), then the irreversible indicator (claims 9 to 11), then the progressive registration travel (claim 12).

Three statutory hooks are claimed because three different parties infringe them: the assembled carrier (claim 1), the thermal module sold on its own as a replacement or refill item (claim 13, drafted with the shell, tray and lid in the preamble so the module itself is what is claimed), and the method of transporting goods (claim 17), which reaches the shipper who packs and closes the carrier.

Claim 17's first step recited peripheral outlet openings 'aligned with the side supply passages' while the passages were first introduced in the following step. That is a plain antecedent-basis defect. Deleting the phrase costs no scope, because the closing step later in the same claim recites the registered position in which the openings overlap the passages.

The 'is not drawn' and 'is omitted' sentences in the FIG. 2 and FIG. 6 briefs were doing legitimate work, telling the pipeline what is hidden, but they are phrased as absences. Since the same preflight rejected an absence-phrased instruction in FIG. 4, I rewrote them as statements of what conceals what and what the view contains, which is more robust and reads better on a sheet.

figures/FIG-1.md: same change to the sentence identifying the three broken-line regions.

figures/FIG-4.md: replaced 'This fragment is taken at a position along that wall between the ledges of the outer shell, so no ledge appears in this view' with a positive description of the wall body's flat inner surface running the height of the fragment.
figures/FIG-5.md: inserted the missing comma in the clause describing the thin upright wall spaced from the wall body, so the spacing and the lower-edge relationship read as two distinct facts.

Claim 17's first step recited peripheral outlet openings 'aligned with the side supply passages' while the passages were first introduced in the following step. That is a plain antecedent-basis defect. Deleting the phrase costs no scope, because the closing step later in the same claim recites the registered position in which the openings overlap the passages.

The 'is not drawn' and 'is omitted' sentences in the FIG. 2 and FIG. 6 briefs were doing legitimate work, telling the pipeline what is hidden, but they are phrased as absences. Since the same preflight rejected an absence-phrased instruction in FIG. 4, I rewrote them as statements of what conceals what and what the view contains, which is more robust and reads better on a sheet.

lines: Condensate management

-A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough formed in the outer shell 10 and extending around the product tray 20. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. Discharge openings 76 are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

+A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough extending around the product tray 20. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. Discharge openings 76 are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

Two thick hatched upright wall bodies joined at the bottom by a thick hatched horizontal bottom body form an upright container, open at the top. A thick hatched horizontal slab across the top ends of both wall bodies is the insulated lid 60, closed. A narrow rib projects downward from its underside inboard of the left wall body top end, and a small compressible body lies between the slab and each top end.

Inside the container, a sectioned open-top box with thin hatched upright walls and a bottom wall is the product tray 20. Its bottom wall is raised above the floor 12 and its outer side surfaces stand clear of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap on each side. Small openings pass through each upright wall below the bottom wall level, and each upright wall stops short of the floor 12.

Two short hatched blocks between the tray bottom wall and the floor 12 are the tray feet 22. The open space between that wall and the floor 12 is the lower return passage 24. A shallow upwardly open trough at the foot of each gap holds an elongated absorbent body.

Two upright plain rectangular blocks, shown schematically, stand within it, spaced from one another and from its ends. The body is open downward at its centre. # FIG. 6

Enlarged schematic sectional view, through a wall of the outer shell, of the mechanical exposure indicator, seen horizontally with the indicator stem in the exposed position. Plain black line work on white, section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.

Plain black line work on white, hatching on cut material, all line work inside the drawing area.

Two thick hatched upright wall bodies joined at the bottom by a thick hatched horizontal bottom body form an upright container open at the top: the sectioned outer shell 10, its bottom body the floor 12. A block with a flat upwardly facing top surface projects inward from each wall body below its top end. A thick hatched horizontal slab across both top ends is the insulated lid 60, closed. A narrow rib projects downward from its underside inboard of the left top end, and a small compressible body lies between the slab and each top end.

Within the container, a sectioned open-top box with thin hatched upright walls and a bottom wall is the product tray 20. Its bottom wall stands above the floor 12 on two short hatched blocks, the tray feet 22, and the space between that wall and the floor 12 is the lower return passage 24. Its upright walls stand clear of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap on each side, stop short of the floor 12, and carry small openings below the bottom wall level. A shallow upwardly open trough at the foot of each gap holds an elongated absorbent body.

Two upright plain rectangular blocks, shown schematically, stand within it, spaced from one another and from its ends. It is open downward at its centre. An open vertical channel runs down through it outboard of each block, opening through its outboard side above the gap and through its downwardly facing lower end above the trough. A small block lies between its underside and the flat top surface of each inward-projecting block, contacting both and flattened between them. A groove opening upward in its top surface receives the lower end of the narrow rib.

An upper left broken-line curve encloses the rib, the groove, the left wall top, the inward-projecting block of the left wall body and the small block on it. A lower left broken-line curve encloses the left outboard channel opening, the left gap and the tray openings. A third curve adjoins it and encloses the lower end of the left channel, its downward opening, the trough and the absorbent body. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

Condensate management

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough extending around the product tray 20. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. Discharge openings 76 are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

# FIG. 1

Schematic vertical section of an assembled passive cold-chain carrier, on a plane cutting through both upright blocks within the module body and the groove in its top surface. Plain black line work on white, hatching on cut material, all line work inside the drawing area.

Two thick hatched upright wall bodies and a thick hatched bottom body joining them form an upright container open at the top: the sectioned outer shell 10, its bottom body the floor 12. Below its top end each wall body carries an inward-projecting block with a flat upwardly facing top surface. A thick hatched horizontal slab across both top ends is the insulated lid 60, closed, a narrow rib projecting down from its underside inboard of the left top end and a small compressible body between it and each top end.

Within it, a sectioned open-top box with thin hatched walls and a bottom wall is the product tray 20, standing above the floor 12 on two short hatched blocks, the tray feet 22, the space beneath it being the lower return passage 24. Its walls stand clear of the wall bodies, leaving an open vertical gap each side, stop short of the floor 12, and carry small openings below bottom wall level. A shallow upwardly open trough at the foot of each gap holds an elongated absorbent body.

Above the product tray 20 and below the lid 60 is an elongated hatched body in section, the thermal module 40, open downward at its centre. Two upright plain rectangular blocks, shown schematically, stand within it, spaced apart and from its ends. An open vertical channel runs down outboard of each block, opening through the body's outboard side above the gap and through its downwardly facing lower end above the trough. A small block, flattened between them, lies between the body underside and each inward-projecting block top surface. A groove opening upward in the top surface receives the lower end of the narrow rib.

Three broken-line curves are drawn: one at the upper left around the rib, groove, left wall top, left inward-projecting block and the small block on it; one at the lower left around the left outboard channel opening, left gap and tray openings; and one adjoining it around the lower end of the left channel, its downward opening, the trough and absorbent body.

- 100: outside the container, lead line to the carrier.

3	Enlarged view of the condensate channel region of FIG. 1, seen horizontally in section. Plain black line work on white, diagonal section hatching on cut material. All line work lies well inside the drawing area, clear of the margins.
4	
5	A thick hatched upright insulating wall body occupies the left portion of the drawing area, running from the upper part of the fragment down to a thick hatched horizontal bottom body that occupies the lower part and extends rightward.
6	
7	In the upper right part of the drawing area, a hatched body fragment is drawn in section. An open vertical channel passes down through this fragment, bounded by hatched material to its left and right. This channel is one of the guide ducts 50. At the lower end of the channel, an opening passes through the downwardly facing bottom surface of the fragment. This opening is one of the discharge openings 76.
8	
9	Below the body fragment, a thin hatched upright wall is drawn in section, spaced to the right of the inner surface of the upright wall body, its lower edge stopping short of the upwardly facing top surface of the horizontal bottom body above the trough described below. A series of small openings passes through this thin upright wall, as in FIG. 1 and FIG. 4. content.text:
All six findings are fixed and the files are back in sync.

- **Condensate channel wording** — `draft/08-detailed-description.md` now reads "A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough extending around the product tray 20." The following sentence already carries the supported fact that the channel and wick remain in the outer shell when the tray is removed, so nothing else moved. Claims 6, 16 and 19 and the figure briefs are untouched.
- **FIG. 1 missing the resilient-foot bearing** — the FIG. 1 brief now draws a small block flattened between the module body underside and the flat top surface of each inward-projecting block of the wall bodies, and the upper left broken-line curve encloses that block and the projection it rests on. Those parts stay unnumbered on FIG. 1 (58 and 18 are labelled on FIG. 3), so they are described generically there.
- **FIG. 1 missing the duct-end discharge opening** — each vertical channel in the module body now opens both through the outboard side above the gap and through its downwardly facing lower end above the trough, and the third curve encloses that lower end, its downward opening, the trough and the absorbent body, adjoining the FIG. 4 curve.
- **FIG. 5 tray wall without perforations** — the thin upright wall in FIG. 5 now carries the same series of small openings shown in FIG. 1 and FIG. 4. No numeral was added to FIG. 5.
- **Curve designations** — FIG. 1 carries FIG. 3, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 just outside the respective curves, and the Brief Description now sends the reader to "the broken-line curve there designated FIG. 3/4/5", with matching opening sentences in the three enlargement briefs. The designations are listed under a separate "View designations" heading, not in the reference-numeral list and not in `numerals.md`, because a view designation is drawing annotation rather than a numeral.
- **Cutting planes** — FIG. 1 is now stated to be taken on a vertical plane cutting transversely through the two phase-change cassettes and through the mating channel, and FIG. 6 on a horizontal plane through the mechanical exposure indicator and a wall of the outer shell, in both the Brief Description and the briefs.

FIG. 1 had to be rewritten compactly to hold the new structure within the brief length limit; every body, contact and opening previously specified is still there, and its numeral list is unchanged.

input.summary: All six review findings are fixed. The description no longer asserts that the condensate channel is formed in the outer shell, which was a structural claim the disclosure does not make. FIG. 1 now depicts the two things its own enlargements showed but it did not: the small block flattened between the module body and each inward-projecting wall block, and the downward opening at the lower end of each vertical channel above the trough. Its three broken-line curves were redrawn to enclose that structure, and they now carry the designations FIG. 3, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 so each region is tied to the view that enlarges it. FIG. 5 now shows the same series of small openings in the tray side wall that FIG. 1 and FIG. 4 show. Both sectional views state their cutting plane in words, in the Brief Description and in the briefs, since no view in the set could carry a section line for FIG. 1. FIG. 1 was rewritten compactly to hold the added structure inside the brief length limit; no body, contact or opening was dropped in doing so, and its numeral list is unchanged. The claims, the numeral table and the disclosed embodiments were not altered.
reasoning: The condensate finding was correct and mattered. The inventor says only that the wick lies in a shallow condensate channel around the product tray, and that the pull tab stays reachable once the tray is out. That supports the channel staying behind with the shell, which is what claims 16 and 19 recite, but it does not support the channel being integral with the shell. I deleted 'formed in the outer shell 10' and left the next sentence, which already says the channel and wick remain in the outer shell when the tray is removed, so no support was lost and no redundancy was added. The trough drawn in the floor body stays a drawing convention confined to the FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 briefs.

For the two cross-view findings I fixed the parent view, not the enlargements. Both the foot bearing on the ledge and the discharge opening at the duct lower end are affirmatively disclosed, so removing them from FIG. 3 and FIG. 5 would have deleted disclosed structure to buy consistency. FIG. 1 gained them instead.

On FIG. 1 those parts are described without their canonical names or numerals, as a small block, an inward-projecting block, and an opening through the downwardly facing lower end of the channel. Every claim limitation, every numbered part (10, 12, 14, 18, 20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 30, 40, 42, 44, 46, 48, 50, 54, 56, 58, 60, 62, 64, 70, 72, 74, 76, 80, 82, 84, 86, 100), and every structure, relationship, result and variant in the Summary, Detailed Description and figure briefs traces to an affirmative USER passage in input/disclosure.md, which is reproduced verbatim as the single USER turn in input/conversation.md. Spot-checks: shell/tray/module/lid and tray feet with lower return passage and two side supply passages ("The product tray is suspended above the shell floor by feet so that a lower return passage remains under the tray. The tray side walls are spaced inward from the shell side walls to form two side supply passages."); spacer frame with central inlet, two downward guide ducts, peripheral outlet openings, and the full circulation path ("Warm air rising from the product region enters the central inlet, divides along faces of the cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage."); passivity ("It has no fan, pump, or powered air mover."); lid-driven registration, gasket-after-registration and resilient-feet/ledge retention (disclosure ¶9); condensate channel, wick, discharge openings and pull tab (¶11); mechanical exposure indicator with stem, temperature-responsive latch, spring, latched exposed position, manual reset only after opening, and no airflow control (¶13); method steps (¶15); optional status of wick and indicator ("The wick and the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator are supported optional features."). Dependent claims 2–12, 14–16 and 18–20 each map to one of those passages. Title, "Not applicable" cross-reference and "Not applicable" government-support statement match input/brief.md ("No priority claim. No federally sponsored research or development."). Background prior-art characterisations are outside this pass. No drafting note, placeholder, open question or unresolved alternative remains in any file. No untraced-item finding is reported.

Depiction conventions accepted as non-substantive: the schematic shell/lid slabs and open-frame body of FIG. 1–FIG. 3; the "plain closed box, shown schematically" cassettes; the "shown schematically" ledge block, resilient-foot blocks, wick body and indicator housing outline. None of these is echoed in the application text as an example shape or optional embodiment, and the claims and description stay shape-neutral, so none is reported.

INTERNAL-CONSISTENCY AND SECTION-LINE RESULT - 5 findings

The named-view designation chain is correct for the three enlargements: FIG. 1's "View designations" list, the FIG. 1 entry in 07-drawings.md ("indicating by three broken-line curves, each designated with the figure that enlarges it") and the opening line of each of FIG-3.md, FIG-4.md and FIG-5.md all use the same repeated designations FIG. 3, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5. Five defects were verified elsewhere:

1. (major, internal_logic) The FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 enlargement regions are placed as adjoining curves on the same left side of FIG. 1, but the two briefs enclose the same left-hand vertical corridor over the same elevation range - FIG. 4 runs from the module's outboard outlet opening down to the lower return passage at the floor, and FIG. 5 runs from the module's downward discharge opening down to the trough at the floor. Two adjoining, non-overlapping curves cannot enclose both.

2. (major, internal_logic) FIG-6.md adds an "upright plain rectangular block … This block is the first phase-change cassette 44" directly inboard of side wall 14 with the indicator stem's inner end touching it. The FIG. 6 entry in 07-drawings.md lists only the stem, latch and spring. The geometry also contradicts FIG. 2 and FIG. 3, where cassette 44 is separated from the shell side wall by a guide duct, the frame's long side wall and the side supply passage, and it implies a stem crossing side supply passage 28 - contrary to claim 11 and to the statement that the indicator "neither opens, closes nor throttles … the side supply passages 28".

3. (major, formalities) FIG. 6 is designated a sectional view "taken on a horizontal plane through the mechanical exposure indicator and a wall of the outer shell", but no view carries a cutting-plane line, and the plane is described in words rather than by a repeated designation, unlike the properly designated FIG. 3/4/5 enlargement curves. (FIG. 1's word-described plane is acceptable because no view of the assembled carrier exists from which to cut it.)

4. (minor, internal_logic) Claims 1 and 13 recite the peripheral outlet openings as already "aligned with the side supply passages" in the module element while the same claims require the indexing rib to shift the module into the registered position "in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages". The description carries the same double statement.

5. (minor, formalities) FIG-1.md states that the section plane cuts "through both upright blocks within the module body" and that hatching is applied to cut material, yet draws those blocks "plain".

Note on scope: the drafting brief records that no prior-art search was run, so the art on file may be incomplete; that is outside this preflight, and Background characterisations are traced by the later citation review.

## Mechanical checks that did not pass

- **Source fidelity is clean before rendering** (fail): SOURCE LEDGER - RESULT

The substantive ledger traces clean. Every claim limitation, every numbered part (10, 12, 14, 18, 20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 30, 40, 42, 44, 46, 48, 50, 54, 56, 58, 60, 62, 64, 70, 72, 74, 76, 80, 82, 84, 86, 100), and every structure, relationship, result and variant in the Summary, Detailed Description and figure briefs traces to an affirmative USER passage in input/disclosure.md, which is reproduced verbatim as the single USER turn in input/conversation.md. The tray side walls are spaced inward from the shell side walls to form two side supply passages."); spacer frame with central inlet, two downward guide ducts, peripheral outlet openings, and the full circulation path ("Warm air rising from the product region enters the central inlet, divides along faces of the cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage."); passivity ("It has no fan, pump, or powered air mover."); lid-driven registration, gasket-after-registration and resilient-feet/ledge retention (disclosure ¶9); condensate channel, wick, discharge openings and pull tab (¶11); mechanical exposure indicator with stem, temperature-responsive latch, spring, latched exposed position, manual reset only after opening, and no airflow control (¶13); method steps (¶15); optional status of wick and indicator ("The wick and the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator are supported optional features."). Dependent claims 2–12, 14–16 and 18–20 each map to one of those passages. Title, "Not applicable" cross-reference and "Not applicable" government-support statement match input/brief.md ("No priority claim. No federally sponsored research or development."). B
  - FIG. 1's FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 enlargement curves enclose the same region
  - FIG. 6 adds phase-change cassette 44 against the shell wall, contradicting FIG. 2, FIG. 3 and claim 11
  - FIG. 6 is designated a sectional view but no view carries the corresponding section line
