11	Three findings remain: one major untraced structural addition to the spacer frame that appears in two briefs (an "outward step" carrying the resilient feet, plus the stepped frame profile in FIG. 1), one minor untraced proportion statement about the functional condensate trough, and one minor formatting defect in FIG-6.md where the section-designation label list sits under no heading. 21	  - Untraced width-to-depth proportion stated for the condensate channel trough

25	
26	- **[major] Untraced "outward step" on the spacer frame side walls and stepped frame profile** (figures/FIG-2.md line 17; figures/FIG-1.md line 9) - The FIG. 2 brief adds a specific structural feature to the spacer frame that the inventor never disclosed: an outward step on each long side wall whose downwardly facing surface carries the resilient feet. FIG. 1 carries the matching profile statement that the frame body "continu[es] down inboard" of that step. The disclosure states only that the closing movement "presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the shell"; it says nothing about a step, about the frame overhanging outboard, or about the frame profile continuing downward inboard of the foot. This is the load-carrying retention joint, so the added step and the inboard/outboard profile convey technical substance and are not saved by "shown schematically": the feet can equally depend from the outboard side of the frame wall directly above the ledge. Note that the corresponding statements in FIG-3.md ("a small block lies between a downwardly facing outboard surface of the sectioned spacer frame 42 and the upwardly facing top surface of the ledge 18, contacting both and flattened between them") and in the Detailed Description ("Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 ... closure ... compresses the resilient feet 58 between the spacer frame 42 and the ledges 18") are fully traced and need no change.

In figures/FIG-1.md, delete the trailing clause so the sentence reads: "A small block is flattened between a down-facing outboard surface of the body and each projecting block." FIG. 1 no longer states that the module body continues down inboard of the foot, so the sentence now ends with the small block flattened between a down-facing outboard surface of the body and each projecting block. FIG. 5 drops the width-to-depth proportion for the condensate trough, which is now a shallow upwardly open trough drawn in section, shown schematically, keeping its position outboard of the tray wall and below the discharge opening 76. FIG. 6 now carries the heading Other labels shown on this figure above the section-designation bullet, with the doubled blank line collapsed. reasoning: The outward step was a structural feature I had added to the spacer frame across two briefs, and it decided how the retention joint is built. The disclosure says only that the closing movement presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the shell, which leaves open whether the feet depend from a step, from a plain outboard face, or from a boss. Reducing FIG. 2 to a downwardly facing outboard surface keeps the one relationship the source gives, a surface from which the feet press down onto the ledge, and stops the drawing from settling the rest.

The FIG. 1 clause about the body continuing down inboard was the matching profile statement, so it had to go with the step. Its removal costs nothing the sheet needs: the small block is still flattened between the body's down-facing outboard surface and the projecting block, which is the contact FIG. 3 and the Detailed Description already describe.

FIG. 3 and the description were left alone deliberately. They state the flattened foot between a downwardly facing outboard surface of the frame and the upwardly facing ledge top, which the reviewer traced as supported, and editing them to match a figure would have inverted the authority order.

The trough proportion was an unhedged dimensional statement about a functional collection feature. The inventor gives only the word shallow, which the brief still uses; wider than it is deep added a ratio the source never supplied and, unlike the wick and tab in the same paragraph, carried no schematic tag. Replacing it with the schematic marker keeps the trough drawable without asserting its section.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is nothing to cite, nothing to distinguish and no reference vocabulary to avoid; the Background carries no citation and there is no characterisation for a citation review to test. The Background states the problem in the inventor's own terms: the temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is laid against a payload, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on an alignment the packer must produce by hand, the condensate left by repeated opening of a reusable carrier, and the erasure of an excursion once the refrigerant recovers. Each states the technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the solution appears in the Detailed Description in the same words the claims use, which is what a later argument would be built from. The distinguishing weight remains on lid-driven registration: the closing travel of the lid shifting the thermal module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so the alignment the passive circulation path depends on is produced by an act the packer cannot skip. The secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator, which reports the state of the refrigerant itself and survives its recovery, and the wick in a condensate channel serviced by a pull tab without opening or removing a cassette. This turn removed untraced frame structure and one dimensional statement from the figure briefs and fixed a heading, so no claim scope moved; claims 2, 14 and 18 still recite the resilient feet pressed against the ledges without reciting how the frame carries them. As the drafting brief records, no prior-art search was run, so the claims have never been measured against a real reference and a search should be run before filing.

content:
The current draft did not pass the automatic filing gate.

Read review/previous-qa.md, then fix every listed mechanical check and every independently
verified finding. Do not argue with a finding in the structured response. If wording triggered a
false positive, make the draft unambiguous enough that the check passes without changing the
invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or
supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

If a figure brief is over-specified, shorten it by removing invented rendering constraints while
preserving the authoritative text, numeral table, disclosed geometry, and required relationships.
Replace generic negative linework controls with positive descriptions of the required bodies,
edges, contacts, openings, and paths. Do not ban second boundaries, parallel lines, inner lines,
rims, ledges, or chamfers merely to suppress a prior rendering artifact.
Remove generic face-linework controls such as prescribing one stroke for every outline or a
shared edge drawn once. Keep only the positive physical geometry and relationship.
For an endpoint finding, choose a broad interior target on the intended part whenever possible.
Remove exact midpoint, depth, quarter, or toward-an-end modifiers that are not disclosure-grounded
or necessary to distinguish the intended part. Replace ordinal geometry references with explicit
outermost, middle, innermost, left, or right terms whenever the order could be read in more than
one direction.

Leave no note, placeholder, question, or instruction for a person. Return the structured answer
with `action` set to "revised" and `questions` as an empty array.

The Background states the problem in the inventor's own terms: the temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is laid against a payload, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on an alignment the packer must produce by hand, the condensate left by repeated opening of a reusable carrier, and the erasure of an excursion once the refrigerant recovers. Each states the technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the solution appears in the Detailed Description in the same words the claims use, which is what a later argument would be built from. The secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator, which reports the state of the refrigerant itself and survives its recovery, and the wick in a condensate channel serviced by a pull tab without opening or removing a cassette. The shell upper edge is now the top end surface of the upright wall body rather than the flat top end surface, so the seal boundary is no longer given a profile, while the disclosed compression of the gasket between the lid underside and the upper edge is kept. Both edits are subtractive and confined to that brief, which now stands at 2692 characters. reasoning: Both words were doing quiet technical work on interfaces the invention depends on. A ledge face called flat is a face declared untapered and horizontal, and a shell edge called flat is a seal boundary declared neither grooved nor stepped nor chamfered. The disclosure gives the existence of the ledge and the fact that the gasket seals against the upper edge, and says nothing about either profile, so neither word could stand as a depiction convention.

I kept upwardly facing on the ledge because it is entailed: the feet are pressed down onto the ledge, so the surface they meet must face up. That is a direction the disclosed action forces, not a profile the drawing chose.

The compression language stays in both sentences. Flattened between them describes what the compressible gasket and the resilient foot do, which the disclosure states directly, and it is what makes the contact readable on the sheet.

I left the plain rectangular cassette slabs in FIG. 2 alone. They are the schematic outline of a part the inventor affirmatively discloses, the reviewer accepted them as a convention, and the word there describes the slab body rather than a functional contact or seal face.

Nothing in draft/ needed touching. The description says only that the gasket bears against the upper edge and that the ledges lie beneath the resilient feet, which is correct and profile-neutral, and amending the text to match a drawing would invert the authority order. Both edits shortened the brief, so no compensating compression was needed and no numeral or leader target moved.

data.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is nothing to cite, nothing to distinguish and no reference vocabulary to avoid; the Background carries no citation and there is no characterisation for a citation review to test. The Background states the problem in the inventor's own terms: the temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is laid against a payload, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on an alignment the packer must produce by hand, the condensate left by repeated opening of a reusable carrier, and the erasure of an excursion once the refrigerant recovers. Each states the technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the solution appears in the Detailed Description in the same words the claims use, which is what a later argument would be built from. The distinguishing weight remains on lid-driven registration: the closing travel of the lid shifting the thermal module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so the alignment the passive circulation path depends on is produced by an act the packer cannot skip. The secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator, which reports the state of the refrigerant itself and survives its recovery, and the wick in a condensate channel serviced by a pull tab without opening or removing a cassette. This turn deleted two words from one figure brief, so no claim scope moved; claims 2, 3, 14 and 18 still recite the feet pressed against the ledges and the gasket sealing after registration without reciting any face profile. As the drafting brief records, no prior-art search was run, so the claims have never been measured against a real reference and a search should be run before filing.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is nothing to cite, nothing to distinguish and no reference vocabulary to avoid; the Background carries no citation and there is no characterisation for a citation review to test. The Background states the problem in the inventor's own terms: the temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is laid against a payload, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on an alignment the packer must produce by hand, the condensate left by repeated opening of a reusable carrier, and the erasure of an excursion once the refrigerant recovers. Each states the technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the solution appears in the Detailed Description in the same words the claims use, which is what a later argument would be built from. The distinguishing weight remains on lid-driven registration: the closing travel of the lid shifting the thermal module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so the alignment the passive circulation path depends on is produced by an act the packer cannot skip. The secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator, which reports the state of the refrigerant itself and survives its recovery, and the wick in a condensate channel serviced by a pull tab without opening or removing a cassette. This turn corrected one leader instruction and removed one redundant bullet, so no claim scope moved. As the drafting brief records, no prior-art search was run, so the claims have never been measured against a real reference and a search should be run before filing.

Read review/previous-qa.md, then fix every listed mechanical check and every independently

false positive, make the draft unambiguous enough that the check passes without changing the
invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or
supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

If a figure brief is over-specified, shorten it by removing invented rendering constraints while
preserving the authoritative text, numeral table, disclosed geometry, and required relationships.
Replace generic negative linework controls with positive descriptions of the required bodies,
edges, contacts, openings, and paths. Do not ban second boundaries, parallel lines, inner lines,
rims, ledges, or chamfers merely to suppress a prior rendering artifact.
Remove generic face-linework controls such as prescribing one stroke for every outline or a
shared edge drawn once. Keep only the positive physical geometry and relationship.
For an endpoint finding, choose a broad interior target on the intended part whenever possible.
Remove exact midpoint, depth, quarter, or toward-an-end modifiers that are not disclosure-grounded
or necessary to distinguish the intended part. Replace ordinal geometry references with explicit
outermost, middle, innermost, left, or right terms whenever the order could be read in more than

1	# Previous review - verdict: fail
2	
3	SCOPE AND AUTHORITY. The only inventor authority is input/disclosure.md and the single USER passage in input/conversation.md, whose text is verbatim identical to the disclosure. The one YOU passage (describing edits that made each tray wall "continu[e] below the bottom wall to a lower edge spaced above the floor 12 just inboard of the trough") is drafting-agent context, never support; I confirmed the current FIG-1 and FIG-5 briefs do NOT verbalize that undisclosed tray-wall extension, so nothing untraced survives from it. input/brief.md was used only for title, applicant/inventor, no-priority and no-government-support formalities.
4	
5	LEDGER RESULT. Every numbered part traces to an affirmative disclosure passage. The numeral table has 31 entries (10, 12, 14, 18, 20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 30, 40, 42, 44, 46, 48, 50, 54, 56, 58, 60, 62, 64, 70, 72, 74, 76, 80, 82, 84, 86, 100); each maps to a part the inventor named (shell/floor/side walls/ledges; tray/feet/return passage/tray side walls/side supply passages/perforations; module/spacer frame/two cassettes/central inlet/guide ducts/peripheral outlets/mating channel/resilient feet; lid/indexing rib/gasket; condensate channel/wick/pull tab/discharge openings; indicator/stem/latch/spring). No numeral is invented, none is reused for two things, every numeral used in text or a brief appears in the table, and every table numeral appears on at least one sheet.
6	
7	CLAIM-BY-CLAIM TRACE. Claims 1-20 were traced limitation by limitation. Independent claims 1, 13 and 17 restate the disclosed carrier, module and method. Dependent limitations trace as follows: cl. 2/14/18 resilient feet pressed against ledges ("presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the shell so that the module cannot lift away from the tray"); cl. 3/18 gasket sealing after registration ("A compressible lid gasket seals against the upper edge of the shell after registration"); cl. 4 confronting inner faces across a central space ("two opposed phase-change cassettes"; "divides along faces of the cassettes"); cl. 5 removable cassettes ("conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame"); cl. 6/19 shallow condensate channel around the tray with removable wick; cl. 7/16 discharge openings at the lower ends of the guide ducts; cl. 8/19 pull tab accessible with the tray removed, wick replaced without opening a cassette; cl. 9/20 stem thermally coupled to one cassette, latch, spring, softening release; cl. 10/20 latched exposed position persisting after cooling, manual reset only after opening; cl. 11 indicator does not control airflow; cl. 12 progressive engagement (entailed by the disclosed order: registration first, gasket seal against the upper edge afterwards); cl. 15 upward-opening channel at the frame top (entailed by a depending lid rib entering it as the lid closes). No dependent claim adds untraced matter; no means-plus-function language; three statutory-class groups as the brief directs.
8	
9	FIGURE BRIEFS. All seven briefs depict only disclosed parts. Depiction conventions are properly confined to the briefs and flagged "shown schematically" (spacer-frame outline, cassette slabs, ledge top surface, groove, resilient-foot blocks, trough, wick, pull tab, indicator outline, stem end, latch block, spring). The functional-surface statements I checked closely are each entailed by an affirmative passage rather than invented: gasket "contacting both and flattened between them" (from "compressible... seals against the upper edge"); resilient foot "flattened between" the frame's outboard down-facing surface and the ledge's upward-facing top surface (from "presses resilient feet... against ledges"); rib "extending below the level of the top end" and inboard of the gasket (from a depending rib entering a channel of a frame that sits inside the shell, with the seal occurring after registration); peripheral outlet "at the foot of the channel" opening sideways into the space that continues down as the side supply passage (from "peripheral outlet openings aligned with the side supply passages" and the disclosed flow order); discharge opening through the downwardly facing bottom surface above the trough (from "Openings at the lower ends of the guide ducts discharge condensate into the channel"); perforations at the tray wall/bottom-wall junction (the only junction where the disclosed passage-to-under-tray route can pass "through perforations in the product tray"). No brief verbalizes taper, angle, relative depth, runout direction, or which end is deeper. No brief or application sentence says an outline is shown "by way of example" or that a member may have "any closed outline".
10	
11	INTERNAL CONSISTENCY. Claims, Summary, Detailed Description and Abstract use the same relationships and the same terms (registered position, overlap/align, circulation path order). A passive cold-chain carrier is disclosed in which the closing of the lid, rather than the care of the packer, establishes the circulation path.

In one aspect, the carrier includes an insulated outer shell having a floor and side walls, a product tray removably received in the outer shell, a thermal module removably received in the outer shell above the product tray, and an insulated lid. The product tray is supported above the floor by tray feet so that a lower return passage remains between the product tray and the floor, and the tray side walls are spaced inward from the side walls of the outer shell to form two side supply passages. The thermal module includes a rigid spacer frame and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame, the spacer frame defining a central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings. The insulated lid carries a depending indexing rib positioned to enter a mating channel of the spacer frame as the lid closes and to shift the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages.

In the registered position the shell, the product tray, the thermal module and the lid cooperate to define a circulation path along which air rising from a product region within the product tray enters the central inlet opening, divides along faces of the two phase-change cassettes, descends through the guide ducts, enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage. The carrier is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover.

The technical effect of lid-driven registration is that the alignment on which the circulation path depends is created by an act the packer cannot omit. The thermal module is placed in the outer shell above the product tray, and the depending indexing rib entering the mating channel shifts the module into the position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages. The seal made by a compressible lid gasket against the upper edge of the outer shell occurs after registration, so the carrier is not closed against a module that is still out of position. The same closing movement presses resilient feet of the spacer frame against ledges of the outer shell, so that the registered module is held down against the product tray and cannot lift away from it during transport.

In a further aspect, a shallow condensate channel extends around the product tray and receives a removable absorbent wick. Discharge openings at lower ends of the guide ducts deliver condensate into the condensate channel. A pull tab on the absorbent wick remains accessible when the product tray is removed, so the wick is replaced without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service.

In a further aspect, the outer shell carries a mechanical exposure indicator visible from outside the carrier. An indicator stem is thermally coupled to one of the phase-change cassettes and is retained by a temperature-responsive latch. If that cassette softens enough to release the latch, a spring moves the indicator stem to a latched exposed position, and the indication remains exposed after the cassette cools again, being reset manually only after the carrier is opened. The indicator therefore reports the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends, survives recovery of the cassette, and requires no battery. The exposure indicator does not control airflow, so the circulation path is unaffected by whether the indicator has tripped.

In a further aspect, a method includes fitting conditioned phase-change cassettes to the spacer frame, placing product in the product tray, placing the product tray in the outer shell, placing the thermal module above the product tray, and closing the insulated lid so that the depending indexing rib enters the mating channel and shifts the thermal module into the registered position, whereafter air circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover.

The features summarised above may be used together or separately, and the summary is not a statement of the scope of the claims.

The finding is fixed in the two figure briefs.

- **FIG. 5 outboard opening** — the duct paragraph now adds "Where that channel meets the open vertical space below, a further opening passes through the outboard face of the module body, so that the channel also opens sideways into that space, as in FIG. 4." The right-hand duct is therefore drawn with the same outboard outlet that FIG. 1, FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 give every duct, matching the disclosed peripheral outlet openings aligned with the side supply passages. The opening is drawn but carries no numeral on this sheet, so FIG. 5 keeps its five numerals and 54 stays labelled on FIG. 4.
- **FIG. 1 curve contents** — the lower right list now begins "the outboard channel opening, the channel lower end and downward opening", so the region marked for enlargement encloses everything FIG. 5 draws, mirroring the lower left list.

While making the first edit I also removed a contradiction it would otherwise have created: both FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 described the channel as bounded by hatched material on its left and right while also passing openings through those faces. Both now read "with hatched material on each side of it apart from the openings described below."

FIG. 5 now draws the outboard opening at the foot of its guide duct, stating that where the channel meets the open vertical space below, a further opening passes through the outboard face of the module body so the channel also opens sideways into that space, as in FIG. 4. The opening is drawn without a numeral, so the sheet keeps its five numerals and 54 remains labelled on FIG. 4. The FIG. 1 lower right curve list now begins with the outboard channel opening, so the marked region encloses everything FIG. 5 draws, mirroring the lower left list. While making that edit I removed a contradiction it would otherwise have created in both FIG. 4 and FIG. 5, which described the channel as bounded by hatched material on each side while also passing openings through those faces; both now read with hatched material on each side of it apart from the openings described below. No file in draft/ changed, numeral coverage still matches the 31 table entries exactly in both directions, all seven briefs are within the length limit with FIG. 2 longest at 2747 characters, and no placeholder or em dash remains.
reasoning: This was a cure by addition rather than deletion, which is unusual for this file but correct here: the peripheral outlet openings are plural in the disclosure and aligned with the side supply passages, so both ducts must discharge sideways. FIG. 5 was the only sheet that closed one of them, so drawing the opening brings the sheet up to the claims rather than trimming the claims down to the sheet.

I left the opening unnumbered on FIG. 5. Numeral 54 is labelled on FIG. 4, the view the description cites for it, and adding it here would have put a sixth numeral on the sheet for no gain and invited a mismatch with the description's statement about where that opening is seen. The brief describes the opening positively and refers to FIG. 4, which is how the other briefs handle structure they show but do not label.

The FIG. 1 curve list had to follow, because an enlargement can only show what the parent view marks. Adding the outboard channel opening to the lower right list makes that region symmetric with the lower left one, which already included it.

The bounded by hatched material to its left and right phrasing was a latent contradiction in both FIG. 4 and FIG. 5: a channel cannot be closed on both sides and also open through them. FIG. 4 had carried that tension since its outlet sentence was added, and inserting a second opening into FIG. 5 would have sharpened it, so I corrected both to say the material lies on each side apart from the openings described. That is a positive statement of the geometry, not a linework ban.

Nothing in draft/ needed changing. The claims already recite peripheral outlet openings aligned with the side supply passages, the description already places one such opening in FIG. 4, and the numeral table is unaffected.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is nothing to cite, nothing to distinguish and no reference vocabulary to avoid; the Background carries no citation and there is no characterisation for a citation review to test. The Background states the problem in the inventor's own terms: the temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is laid against a payload, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on an alignment the packer must produce by hand, the condensate left by repeated opening of a reusable carrier, and the erasure of an excursion once the refrigerant recovers. Each states the technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the solution appears in the Detailed Description in the same words the claims use, which is what a later argument would be built from. The distinguishing weight remains on lid-driven registration: the closing travel of the lid shifting the thermal module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so the alignment the passive circulation path depends on is produced by an act the packer cannot skip. This turn improves the drawing support for that feature, because both ducts are now shown discharging into their side supply passages as the claims require. The secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator, which reports the state of the refrigerant itself and survives its recovery, and the wick in a condensate channel serviced by a pull tab without opening or removing a cassette. No claim scope moved. As the drafting brief records, no prior-art search was run, so the claims have never been measured against a real reference and a search should be run before filing.

The finding is fixed in `figures/FIG-1.md`.

- The module is now described with the topology FIG. 2 states: "Above the tray, below the lid 60, a sectioned hatched body is the thermal module 40: two cut upright side portions joined by a hatched bottom, the space between the side portions open at the top beneath the lid 60, the bottom open downward at its centre, the body holding two upright hatched blocks, shown schematically, spaced apart." The module can no longer be drawn as a closed-top body with a continuous roof.
- The groove sentence now reads "A groove opening upward in the cut top surface of the left side portion takes the rib's lower end", so the mating channel sits on a cut side wall top edge, matching FIG. 2's placement of it on the top edge of the near long side wall.

The rest of the paragraph already presupposed that topology and is unchanged: the bottom open downward at its centre is the central inlet opening, the channel's downward lower end over the trough is the discharge opening through the same bottom, and the down-facing outboard surface is the surface FIG. 2 gives the frame.

No file in `draft/` changed, since none of them recites a top surface of the spacer frame. FIG. 1 is now 2742 characters, all seven briefs are within the length limit, numeral coverage still matches the 31 table entries exactly in both directions, and no placeholder or em dash remains.

input.summary: The finding is fixed in figures/FIG-1.md. The thermal module is now described as a sectioned body of two cut upright side portions joined by a hatched bottom, with the space between them open at the top beneath the lid and the bottom open downward at its centre, so FIG. 1 carries the same open-top frame topology that FIG. 2 states and can no longer be rendered as a closed-top body with a continuous roof. The groove that receives the rib is now placed in the cut top surface of the left side portion, matching FIG. 2's placement of the mating channel on the top edge of a long side wall. The rest of the paragraph already presupposed that topology and is unchanged. No file in draft/ changed, FIG. 1 is now 2742 characters, all seven briefs are within the length limit, numeral coverage still matches the 31 table entries exactly in both directions, and no placeholder or em dash remains.
reasoning: This was a cross-brief topology conflict rather than a source problem. Each sheet renders from its own brief, so FIG. 1 saying the top surface in the singular let the module be drawn as an inverted U with a roof, while FIG. 2 explicitly gives the frame an open top with a bottom panel. Two sheets would then show spacer frame 42 as two different objects.

Aligning FIG. 1 to FIG. 2 adds nothing to the invention. The open-top frame is already asserted in FIG. 2, it is inherent in the disclosed term rigid spacer frame, and FIG. 1's other module statements already depended on it: the bottom open downward at its centre is the central inlet opening, the channel's downward lower end over the trough is the discharge opening through that same bottom, and the down-facing outboard surface is the one FIG. 2 gives the frame. Only the top was left ambiguous, and that is what I closed.

Placing the groove in the cut top surface of the left side portion follows from the same topology: with no roof, the only top surface the section can show is the cut edge of a side wall, which is exactly where FIG. 2 puts the mating channel.

I left draft/ alone. Neither the claims nor the description recites a top surface of the spacer frame, so there was nothing there to conform, and editing the text to match a drawing would invert the authority order.
The rewrite lengthened FIG. 1 to 2742 characters, still inside the limit, so no compensating compression was needed and no numeral, leader target or curve content moved.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references, so there is nothing to cite, nothing to distinguish and no reference vocabulary to avoid; the Background carries no citation and there is no characterisation for a citation review to test. The Background states the problem in the inventor's own terms: the temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is laid against a payload, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on an alignment the packer must produce by hand, the condensate left by repeated opening of a reusable carrier, and the erasure of an excursion once the refrigerant recovers. Each states the technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the solution appears in the Detailed Description in the same words the claims use, which is what a later argument would be built from. The distinguishing weight remains on lid-driven registration: the closing travel of the lid shifting the thermal module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so the alignment the passive circulation path depends on is produced by an act the packer cannot skip. This turn improves the drawing support for that feature, because FIG. 1 now shows the frame open at the top where the rib enters the channel, consistent with FIG. 2. The secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator, which reports the state of the refrigerant itself and survives its recovery, and the wick in a condensate channel serviced by a pull tab without opening or removing a cassette. No claim scope moved. As the drafting brief records, no prior-art search was run, so the claims have never been measured against a real reference and a search should be run before filing.

content:
The current draft did not pass the automatic filing gate.

Read review/previous-qa.md, then fix every listed mechanical check and every independently
verified finding. Do not argue with a finding in the structured response. If wording triggered a
false positive, make the draft unambiguous enough that the check passes without changing the
invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or
supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

If a figure brief is over-specified, shorten it by removing invented rendering constraints while
preserving the authoritative text, numeral table, disclosed geometry, and required relationships.
Replace generic negative linework controls with positive descriptions of the required bodies,
edges, contacts, openings, and paths. Do not ban second boundaries, parallel lines, inner lines,
rims, ledges, or chamfers merely to suppress a prior rendering artifact.

content.text:
I ran the full text-side gate. The reviewer's findings list is empty, and my own pass confirms the filing text is clean, so I changed nothing.

**Verification results**

- Numerals: `draft/numerals.md` holds 31 entries; the union of numerals labelled across the seven briefs is exactly those 31, and no brief labels a numeral outside the table. Both directions match.
- Per-sheet load: FIG. 1 has 7, FIG. 2 has 8, FIG. 3 has 7, FIG. 4 has 6, FIG. 5 has 5, FIG. 6 has 4, FIG. 7 has 6. None exceeds the eight-per-sheet limit.
- Figure numbering: the Brief Description carries entries FIG. 1 through FIG. 7 with no gap, and seven brief files exist with matching names.
- Text-to-drawing: every "seen in FIG. n", "Referring to FIG. n" and "FIG. 6 shows" statement names parts the cited brief actually lists.
- Designation chains: "line 7-7" appears in the FIG. 6 brief, the FIG. 7 brief and both Brief Description entries; the FIG. 3, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 enlargement designations appear in each enlargement brief and in all three Brief Description entries.
- Formalities and hygiene: abstract is a single paragraph of 141 words; every brief is within the length limit, FIG. 2 longest at 2747 characters; no placeholder, note, question or em dash anywhere in `draft/` or `figures/`.

**Why the gate still fails.** Both remaining blockers are the same fact: no drawing sheet exists for FIG. 1 through FIG. 7, which is why all 31 numerals are reported absent from every drawing. `figures/` contains only the seven Markdown briefs. Sheets are produced from those briefs by the image pipeline, and I am not permitted to write PNG or SVG files, so I cannot regenerate them or produce OCR, leader-endpoint or hatch evidence from here; `review/figure-audit-evidence.json` does not exist either. The reviewer reached the same conclusion and added that the drawing plan itself is complete, so rendering the briefs as written should clear both checks without touching the filing text.

I did not act on the reviewer's closing observation about my earlier report of FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 tray-wall geometry. That geometry was removed from the briefs several rounds ago as untraced; the files on disk now show the tray box with its walls meeting the bottom wall and the perforations at that junction, consistent with FIG. 4, the description and claims 1, 13 and 17. The mismatch is between a stale conversation message and the current files, not a defect in the files.

The application cannot be published until the sheets render and pass inspection.

reasoning: The request was to run the gate and publish only after every blocker clears. The blockers do not clear, so the correct outcome is to report that plainly rather than to edit clean text in order to make a check go quiet. Editing the filing text would not create a drawing sheet.

All pass, which matches the reviewer's independent text-level trace.

That is correct and expected: the tray wall extending below the bottom wall to an edge above the floor was removed as untraced several rounds ago, and the current briefs show the tray box with its walls meeting the bottom wall and the perforations at that junction, consistent with FIG. 4, the description and claims 1, 13 and 17. input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references and the draft contains no REF citation, so there is nothing to cite, nothing to distinguish and no characterisation for the citation review to test. The Background's statements about powered carriers, passive carriers, condensate and electronic data loggers are prior-art framing rather than assertions about the invention. It states the problem in the inventor's own terms: the temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is laid against a payload, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on an alignment the packer must produce by hand, the condensate left by repeated opening of a reusable carrier, and the erasure of an excursion once the refrigerant recovers. Each states the technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the solution appears in the Detailed Description in the same words the claims use, which is what a later argument would be built from. The distinguishing weight sits on lid-driven registration: the closing travel of the lid shifting the thermal module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so the alignment the passive circulation path depends on is produced by an act the packer cannot skip. The secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator, which reports the state of the refrigerant itself and survives its recovery, and the wick in a condensate channel serviced by a pull tab without opening or removing a cassette. Nothing changed this turn, so no claim scope moved. As the drafting brief records, no prior-art search was run for this workspace, so the art on file is empty rather than merely incomplete; the claims have never been measured against a real reference and a search should be run before filing.

content:
The current draft did not pass the automatic filing gate.

Read review/previous-qa.md, then fix every listed mechanical check and every independently
verified finding. Do not argue with a finding in the structured response. If wording triggered a
false positive, make the draft unambiguous enough that the check passes without changing the
invention. Keep the reference-numeral table, drawing descriptions, detailed description, claims,
and every file in figures/ synchronized.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add
an implementation detail or embodiment because it appeared in a generated image. For a drawing
finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or
supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

If a figure brief is over-specified, shorten it by removing invented rendering constraints while
preserving the authoritative text, numeral table, disclosed geometry, and required relationships.
Replace generic negative linework controls with positive descriptions of the required bodies,
edges, contacts, openings, and paths. Do not ban second boundaries, parallel lines, inner lines,
rims, ledges, or chamfers merely to suppress a prior rendering artifact.
Remove generic face-linework controls such as prescribing one stroke for every outline or a
shared edge drawn once. Keep only the positive physical geometry and relationship.
For an endpoint finding, choose a broad interior target on the intended part whenever possible.
Remove exact midpoint, depth, quarter, or toward-an-end modifiers that are not disclosure-grounded
or necessary to distinguish the intended part. Replace ordinal geometry references with explicit
outermost, middle, innermost, left, or right terms whenever the order could be read in more than
one direction.

Leave no note, placeholder, question, or instruction for a person. Return the structured answer
with `action` set to "revised" and `questions` as an empty array.

=== field ===

content.content:
1	In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.
2	
3	Overall arrangement
4	
5	Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.
6	
7	The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.
8	
9	The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. One tray side wall 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.
10	
11	The thermal module
12	
13	Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in a mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 before packing.
14	
15	The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, one of which is seen in FIG. 4, each guide duct 50 located beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 positioned to align with the side supply passages 28.
16	
17	The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and the depending indexing rib 62 described below, which enters it from above, are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.
18	
19	Registration and retention by the lid
20	
21	The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into the registered position.
22	
23	This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and the registration is completed by the closing of the lid. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is therefore created by an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.
24	
25	The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, one such ledge 18 and one such resilient foot 58 being seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. Closure of the insulated lid 60 compresses the resilient feet 58 between the spacer frame 42 and the ledges 18, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport.
26	
27	The circulation path
28	
29	In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20.
30	
31	The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Air warmed in the product region rises to the central inlet opening 48, and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes descends through the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, so that circulation proceeds without any powered air mover.
32	
33	Condensate management
34	
35	A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough extending around the product tray 20. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. Discharge openings 76 are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Condensate present in the guide ducts 50 runs down them and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 into the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.
36	
37	The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.
38	
39	Mechanical exposure indicator
40	
41	The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. FIG. 6 shows the mechanical exposure indicator 80 as it appears from outside the outer shell 10. Referring to FIG. 7, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44. FIG. 6 and FIG. 7 show the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position.
42	
43	The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.
44	
45	The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.
46	
47	The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.
48	
49	Operation
50	
51	In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Goods are placed in the product tray 20 and the product tray 20 is placed in the outer shell 10 so that the tray feet 22 stand on the floor 12, leaving the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20 and the two side supply passages 28 between the tray side walls 26 and the side walls 14. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20. The insulated lid 60 is then closed, whereby the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 and shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position, the resilient feet 58 are pressed against the ledges 18 to retain the thermal module 40, and the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. Air thereafter circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.
52	
53	Essential and optional features
54	
55	Two phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42, opposed across the central space. Entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.
56	
57	The described implementations are examples. The optional features identified above may be provided in any combination or omitted, and the described implementations may otherwise be varied within the scope of the claims that follow.
58

The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44. FIG. 6 and FIG. 7 show the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

Operation

In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Goods are placed in the product tray 20 and the product tray 20 is placed in the outer shell 10 so that the tray feet 22 stand on the floor 12, leaving the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20 and the two side supply passages 28 between the tray side walls 26 and the side walls 14. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20. The insulated lid 60 is then closed, whereby the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 and shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position, the resilient feet 58 are pressed against the ledges 18 to retain the thermal module 40, and the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. Air thereafter circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.

Essential and optional features

Two phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42, opposed across the central space. Entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.

The described implementations are examples. The optional features identified above may be provided in any combination or omitted, and the described implementations may otherwise be varied within the scope of the claims that follow.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references and the draft contains no REF citation, so there is nothing to cite, nothing to distinguish and no characterisation for a citation review to test; the Background's statements about powered carriers, passive carriers, condensate and electronic data loggers are prior-art framing rather than assertions about the invention. The Background states the problem in the inventor's own terms: the temperature spread that results when a refrigerant mass is laid against a payload, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on an alignment the packer must produce by hand, the condensate left by repeated opening of a reusable carrier, and the erasure of an excursion once the refrigerant recovers. Each states the technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the solution appears in the Detailed Description in the same words the claims use, which is what a later argument would be built from. The distinguishing weight sits on lid-driven registration: the closing travel of the lid shifting the thermal module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so the alignment the passive circulation path depends on is produced by an act the packer cannot skip, and claim 12 adds the progressive engagement that begins while the lid is still spaced above the shell. The secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator, which reports the state of the refrigerant itself and survives its recovery, and the wick in a condensate channel serviced by a pull tab without opening or removing a cassette. Claim 13 covers the thermal module alone so a replacement module is reached, and claim 17 covers the packing and transport method so the shipper is reached. As the drafting brief records, no prior-art search was run for this workspace, so the art on file is empty rather than merely incomplete; the claims have never been measured against a real reference and a search should be run before filing.

Generated pixels are never authority for the invention. The authority order is the inventor's
disclosure and conversation, then the patent text, then the figure briefs, then the rendered
sheets. Never change the claims, description, numeral table, or disclosed embodiments merely to
excuse geometry, an object, or a leader endpoint that the image model drew incorrectly. Never add

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or

outermost, middle, innermost, left, or right terms whenever the order could be read in more than

=== background paras ===
Passive carriers are attractive because they have no battery to charge, no motor to fail and no electrical approval burden for air transport. They are also harder to control. When a refrigerant mass is simply laid on top of, beside or beneath a payload, the cooled air falls where gravity and the packing arrangement happen to send it. Items directly against the refrigerant are driven toward the cold end of the acceptable band or below it, while items on the far side of the payload sit in a stagnant warm layer. The result is a temperature spread across the payload that grows as the load is packed more densely, and that varies from shipment to shipment because it depends on how a particular packer arranged the goods and the refrigerant on a particular day.
Two further problems attend repeated reuse of a passive carrier. First, moist ambient air admitted each time the carrier is opened condenses on the cold surfaces of the refrigerant mass and runs down into the payload space, wetting labels and cartons and, over many cycles, leaving standing water in the base of the carrier. Where the refrigerant is a sealed cassette, drying the interior often means removing the cassette from service. Second, a passive carrier gives no account of itself. If the payload was exposed to a temperature excursion in transit, and the refrigerant has since recovered, an inspection at the receiving dock shows a cold carrier and a firm cassette, and the excursion leaves no trace. Electronic data loggers record such events but add cost, battery management and a reading step to every unit shipped, and they report a sensor location rather than the state of the refrigerant that the payload actually depends on.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
Temperature-sensitive goods such as vaccines, biological samples, prepared meals and laboratory reagents are frequently shipped in insulated carriers that hold a payload within a target temperature band for a period of hours or days. Carriers of this general kind fall into two broad families. Powered carriers use a fan, a pump or another driven air mover, together with a power source, to force air over a cold source and through the payload space. Passive carriers omit the power source and rely on conduction from, and natural convection around, a refrigerant mass such as water ice, dry ice, gel packs or sealed cassettes charged with a phase-change material.

Passive carriers are attractive because they have no battery to charge, no motor to fail and no electrical approval burden for air transport. They are also harder to control. When a refrigerant mass is simply laid on top of, beside or beneath a payload, the cooled air falls where gravity and the packing arrangement happen to send it. Items directly against the refrigerant are driven toward the cold end of the acceptable band or below it, while items on the far side of the payload sit in a stagnant warm layer. The result is a temperature spread across the payload that grows as the load is packed more densely, and that varies from shipment to shipment because it depends on how a particular packer arranged the goods and the refrigerant on a particular day.

Attempts to impose a defined circulation path on a passive carrier run into a practical difficulty. The path is defined by clearances, by openings and by the alignment between them, and every one of those relationships is destroyed if the component that carries the openings is set down rotated, offset or skewed by a person working quickly at a packing bench. A carrier that circulates air well when it is assembled precisely, and poorly when it is not, delivers the variability it was intended to remove. Packing instructions, printed arrows and keyed corner blocks all depend on the packer looking, and none of them acts on a component that has already been set down out of position.

Two further problems attend repeated reuse of a passive carrier. First, moist ambient air admitted each time the carrier is opened condenses on the cold surfaces of the refrigerant mass and runs down into the payload space, wetting labels and cartons and, over many cycles, leaving standing water in the base of the carrier. Where the refrigerant is a sealed cassette, drying the interior often means removing the cassette from service. Second, a passive carrier gives no account of itself. If the payload was exposed to a temperature excursion in transit, and the refrigerant has since recovered, an inspection at the receiving dock shows a cold carrier and a firm cassette, and the excursion leaves no trace. Electronic data loggers record such events but add cost, battery management and a reading step to every unit shipped, and they report a sensor location rather than the state of the refrigerant that the payload actually depends on.

There remains a need for a reusable passive carrier that establishes the same circulation path around the payload every time it is closed, without a powered air mover and without relying on the care of the person who packed it, that manages the condensate produced by repeated opening without taking the refrigerant out of service, and that retains a visible mechanical record of a refrigerant temperature excursion after the refrigerant has recovered.

All three findings are fixed.

- **Condensate channel allocation** — the Detailed Description now reads "A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the absorbent wick 72 remains in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed", which is the relationship the disclosure states. In `figures/FIG-5.md` the trough is now placed "At the bottom of the space outboard of the thin upright wall, below the discharge opening 76", so the sheet shows the disclosed trough without asserting which body forms it. Claims 16 and 19 were not touched.
- **Background characterisations** — the three assertions are now conditional: passive carriers "need have no battery to charge, no motor to fail and no electrical approval burden for air transport"; "The result can be a temperature spread across the payload that tends to grow as the load is packed more densely, and that may vary from shipment to shipment"; and "Electronic data loggers can record such events, but add cost, battery management and a reading step to every unit shipped". No source was added, and the rest of the Background is unchanged.
- **Naming mismatch** — every occurrence of "the module body" and "this module body" in the FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 briefs is now "the sectioned spacer frame" and "this sectioned spacer frame", matching FIG. 3, the description and claims 7 and 16. That includes the leader entries for 50, 54 and 76. The numeral lists are otherwise unchanged.

While in the two briefs I removed a duplicated "shown schematically" in the FIG. 5 trough sentence and trimmed two phrases in FIG. 4 so both stay within the brief length limit; FIG. 4 is 2772 characters and FIG. 5 is 2734. Numeral coverage still matches the 31 table entries exactly in both directions, and no placeholder or em dash remains.

The two mechanical checks remain open for the same reason as before: no drawing sheet exists for FIG. 1 through FIG. 7, so the 31 numerals are absent from every drawing. `figures/` holds only the Markdown briefs, sheets are rendered from them by the image pipeline, and I cannot write image files.

input.summary: All three reviewer findings are fixed. The Detailed Description now says only that the absorbent wick 72 remains in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed, dropping the assertion that the channel itself stays behind, and the FIG. 5 brief places the trough at the bottom of the space outboard of the thin upright wall below the discharge opening 76 instead of forming it in the shell's bottom body, so neither text nor sheet allocates the channel to a component the disclosure does not name. The three Background characterisations are now conditional, saying passive carriers need have no battery, motor or electrical approval burden, that the result can be a temperature spread that tends to grow with packing density and may vary between shipments, and that loggers can record such events. Every use of module body in the FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 briefs is now the sectioned spacer frame, matching FIG. 3, the description and claims 7 and 16, including the leader entries for 50, 54 and 76. I also removed a duplicated schematic tag in the FIG. 5 trough sentence and trimmed two phrases in FIG. 4 so both briefs stay within the length limit at 2734 and 2772 characters. Numeral coverage still matches the 31 table entries exactly in both directions and no placeholder or em dash remains. The two mechanical checks stay open because no drawing sheet exists for FIG. 1 through FIG. 7; figures/ holds only the Markdown briefs, the image pipeline renders the sheets from them, and I cannot write image files.
reasoning: The condensate finding was right on the narrow point: the inventor places the channel around the product tray and says the pull tab stays reachable once the tray is out, which supports a wick that stays behind but not a channel formed in the shell. Trimming the description to the wick and loosening the FIG. 5 trough to the bottom of the outboard space keeps the disclosed collection route while leaving open which body carries the trough. Claims 16 and 19 recite within the outer shell, a location rather than an allocation, so they needed no edit.

The Background softening costs nothing and removes real exposure. With prior_art/ empty, definite statements about how existing carriers and loggers behave are untraceable, and conditional phrasing still sets up every problem the invention addresses: variable payload spread, condensate on reuse, and an excursion that leaves no trace once the refrigerant recovers.

The naming fix matters because claims 7 and 16 attribute the guide ducts and discharge openings to the spacer frame, not to the module as a whole. Calling the sectioned part the module body in two enlargements invited a reader to associate those features with the frame-plus-cassettes assembly. Aligning on the sectioned spacer frame gives the part one name across FIG. 3, FIG. 4, FIG. 5, the description and the claims.

Both briefs grew with the longer part name, so I recovered the characters inside the same files rather than dropping geometry: a duplicated schematic tag in the FIG. 5 trough sentence and two wordy phrases in FIG. 4. No body, contact, opening, numeral or leader target changed.

The two mechanical checks are not curable from here. They require rendered sheets, the sheets are produced from these briefs by the image pipeline, and creating image files is outside what I am permitted to do, so I state the position plainly rather than altering the filing text to make a drawing check pass.

input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references and the draft contains no REF citation, so there is nothing to cite, nothing to distinguish and no characterisation of a cited source to test. This turn tightens the Background so that its prior-art framing no longer states definite facts about existing carriers and data loggers that no document in the workspace supports; the problems it sets up are unchanged, namely the temperature spread that can result when a refrigerant mass is laid against a payload, the dependence of any imposed circulation path on an alignment the packer must produce by hand, the condensate left by repeated opening of a reusable carrier, and the erasure of an excursion once the refrigerant recovers. Each of those still states the technical problem that a specific claimed feature solves, and the solution appears in the Detailed Description in the same words the claims use, which is what a later argument would be built from. The distinguishing weight sits on lid-driven registration: the closing travel of the lid shifting the thermal module until the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages, so the alignment the passive circulation path depends on is produced by an act the packer cannot skip, with claim 12 adding the progressive engagement that begins while the lid is still spaced above the shell. The secondary positions are the irreversible mechanical exposure indicator, which reports the state of the refrigerant itself and survives its recovery, and the wick in a condensate channel serviced by a pull tab without opening or removing a cassette. Claim 13 reaches a replacement thermal module and claim 17 reaches the shipper who packs and closes the carrier. As the drafting brief records, no prior-art search was run, so the claims have never been measured against a real reference and a search should be run before filing.
